questions.question: Name the three groups of components in an electrical circuit with their roles, describe how a cell, a generator and a solar panel each convert energy, and distinguish voltage from capacity.
questions.expected_answer: Input devices supply electrical energy by converting it from another form; output devices use electrical energy by converting it into light, heat, sound or movement; control devices decide whether and when current flows. A cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy through a reaction between two different electrodes in an electrolyte, giving about 1.5 volts, with several cells forming a battery and rechargeable cells reversing the reaction when charged. A generator converts kinetic energy into electrical energy by moving a coil in a magnetic field, from a bicycle dynamo to a power station alternator. A solar panel of photovoltaic cells converts light energy directly into electrical energy in treated silicon and gives current only while light falls on it, so systems store energy in batteries. Voltage is the push the device gives the charge; capacity or power is how much energy it can supply and how fast, so two devices with equal voltage can differ greatly in what they can run and when.

questions.question: State what each of a lamp, heater, buzzer and motor converts electrical energy into, with an example, explain the role of a resistor and why it is grouped with output devices, and explain why component ratings must match the supply.
questions.expected_answer: A lamp converts electrical energy into light, a filament lamp by heating a tungsten wire until it glows with much waste heat and a light-emitting diode directly from a semiconductor with little heat and current in one direction only; a heater converts it into heat in a coil of nichrome resistance wire in kettles, stoves, geysers and irons; a buzzer converts it into sound through a vibrating diaphragm driven by an electromagnet or piezoelectric crystal, as in alarms; a motor converts it into movement by the force on current-carrying coils in a magnetic field, as in fans, pumps and the Term 3 winder, and run backwards is a generator. A resistor limits current to a safe value for a sensitive component such as a light-emitting diode, has a resistance in ohms shown by coloured bands, and is grouped with output devices because it uses energy, converting a little into heat. Ratings give the voltage and power a device is designed for, and a mismatch destroys or disables it, so a 3 volt bulb on 9 volts burns out and a 12 volt motor on 1.5 volts barely turns.

questions.question: Classify switches by how they are operated, whether they latch, what operates them and how many paths they control, giving an example of each, and explain what a relay does.
questions.expected_answer: By operation: toggle switches flipped by hand on walls, push switches that are push-to-make as in a doorbell or panic button or push-to-break as in a fridge door light, slide switches on torches, rotary switches on stove controls, key switches on ignitions and alarm panels, and rocker switches on power strips. By latching: a latching switch stays in position like a wall switch while a momentary switch returns when released like a doorbell. By what operates them: a reed switch closes near a magnet for door sensors, a tilt switch when tipped, a pressure mat when stood on, a thermostat by temperature using a bending bimetal strip in geysers and irons, a float switch by water level, and a light sensor with a transistor by darkness for streetlights. By paths: single-pole single-throw controls one path on or off, single-pole double-throw connects one wire to either of two as in a two-way staircase switch, and double-pole breaks two wires together as in a main switch. A relay is a switch operated by an electromagnet so a small current in one circuit controls a large current in another, as when a key switch starts a car's motor or a small panic circuit fires a loud siren.
